blocks.x: Knee pain can slowly change your everyday life. Walking, climbing stairs, exercising, or even getting up from a chair can become uncomfortable. For people living with long-term knee pain due to osteoarthritis, cartilage damage, or other joint problems, the fear of eventually needing a knee replacement is also common.
But does every patient with knee pain need knee replacement?
Not always.

Depending on the cause and severity of the knee problem, doctors may consider different treatment options, including physiotherapy, rehabilitation, medicines, injections, and other joint-preservation treatments. Orthosport focuses on preventive, minimally invasive and joint-preservation approaches, including biologic and innovative treatments.
Can Just 1 Injection Give Long-Term Knee Pain Relief?
The idea of “Just 1 Injection for Up to 10 Years of Knee Pain Relief” sounds attractive, especially for someone who has been dealing with knee pain for years.
However, the response to any injection is different for every patient. There is no guarantee that one injection will provide 10 years of pain relief for everyone.
The important question is:
Are you the right candidate for an injection-based treatment?
This depends on several factors, including:
Your age
The cause of your knee pain
The condition of your cartilage
Osteoarthritis severity
MRI and X-ray findings
Your activity level
Knee stability and movement
Previous treatments
Overall condition of the knee

A proper examination and review of your imaging are therefore important before deciding on treatment. The information accompanying Dr. Manu Bora’s video also emphasizes that treatment recommendations depend on individual patient factors.
Adipocyte Stem Cell Injection for Knee Pain
One of the newer approaches discussed for joint preservation is the use of adipose-derived cells/biologics, sometimes referred to as adipocyte stem cell treatment.
The concept is to use biological material derived from the patient’s own body as part of a regenerative or joint-preservation treatment strategy.
Dr. Manu Bora discusses such treatment approaches in the context of patients with chronic knee pain and explains that the appropriate treatment depends on the individual condition of the knee.

The goal is not simply to reduce pain temporarily. The broader aim of joint-preservation treatment is to help selected patients manage symptoms and preserve knee function while considering whether more invasive procedures can be delayed.
A 60-Year-Old Patient With Knee Pain
A recent video from Dr. Manu Bora features a 60-year-old patient and an adipocyte stem cell injection, with the video focusing on the patient’s experience with knee pain and the treatment approach.
Patient stories can be useful for understanding what an individual treatment journey may look like, but one patient’s result should not be taken as a guarantee of the same result for another person.
Every knee is different.
That is why an individual assessment is essential before choosing any injection or procedure.
Does Knee Pain Always Mean Knee Replacement?
No.

Knee pain can have many causes. Osteoarthritis and cartilage damage are common causes, but ligament problems, meniscus injuries, inflammation, muscle weakness, altered movement patterns and other conditions can also contribute to pain.
Treatment should therefore start with understanding why your knee hurts.

In selected cases, conservative care, rehabilitation or joint-preservation treatments may be considered before replacement surgery. Orthosport describes its approach as preventive, proactive and minimally invasive, with a focus on joint preservation.

At the same time, not every patient can or should avoid knee replacement. If the joint has advanced damage and other treatments are no longer appropriate or effective, knee replacement may still be considered.
How Is the Right Treatment Decided?
A knee treatment plan should be based on your actual condition rather than simply your age or pain level.
A typical assessment may include:
1. Understanding Your Symptoms
The doctor may ask about:
How long you have had knee pain
Pain while walking
Pain while climbing stairs
Swelling
Stiffness
Locking or clicking
Difficulty exercising
Previous treatments
2. Reviewing MRI or X-Ray
Imaging can help the specialist understand the condition of the cartilage, bones, meniscus and other structures around the knee.
3. Clinical Knee Examination
Your knee movement, stability, strength and functional limitations can provide additional information.
4. Discussing Treatment Options
After understanding the condition, the doctor can explain whether rehabilitation, medication, injections, biologic treatments or surgery may be appropriate.
Don’t Choose a Treatment Only Because of a Promise
If you are searching online for “knee pain treatment without surgery”, “stem cell injection for knee pain”, or “how to avoid knee replacement,” you will find many different claims.
Be careful with absolute promises.
No single injection is suitable for every patient, and no treatment can guarantee the same duration of pain relief for everyone.
The right approach is to first understand your diagnosis and then discuss the available options with an orthopedic specialist.
Can an Injection Delay Knee Replacement?
For some appropriately selected patients, joint-preservation treatment may be considered with the goal of managing symptoms and potentially delaying more invasive treatment.
But “delay” is different from “guaranteed avoidance.”
Whether knee replacement can be delayed depends on the extent of joint damage, symptoms, functional limitations, response to previous treatment and other individual factors.
This is why an MRI/X-ray review and clinical assessment are important before making a decision.
What Can You Do If You Have Chronic Knee Pain?
If you have been experiencing knee pain for months or years, don’t simply continue taking painkillers or avoid activity without finding the underlying cause.
Start by getting the knee properly assessed.
Depending on your diagnosis, treatment may include:
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation
Strengthening exercises
Weight and activity management where appropriate
Medication when indicated
Injection-based treatments for selected patients
Biologic/joint-preservation approaches
Surgery when clinically necessary

blocks.x: Neck and shoulder pain are common problems that can affect people of all ages. Long hours at a desk, poor posture, excessive mobile-phone use, gym workouts, sports injuries, and everyday stress can all contribute to discomfort in the neck and shoulder region.

While occasional pain may improve with rest, persistent or recurring pain can affect your sleep, work, exercise, and daily activities. Finding the underlying cause and following the right treatment plan can help restore movement and improve function.

At Threads Physio, physiotherapy focuses on understanding the reason behind your pain and creating a personalised rehabilitation plan based on your condition, movement, strength, and daily requirements.
What Causes Neck and Shoulder Pain?
Neck and shoulder pain can develop for many different reasons. Some common causes include:
Poor sitting posture
Long hours working on a computer
Excessive mobile-phone use
Muscle stiffness or weakness
Sports injuries
Shoulder problems
Cervical spine-related conditions
Repetitive movements
Heavy lifting
Poor exercise technique
Previous injuries
Lack of mobility and strength
In some cases, pain may also travel from the neck towards the shoulder, arm, or upper back. Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arm may indicate that a more detailed assessment is required.
Common Symptoms of Neck and Shoulder Pain
People with neck and shoulder problems may experience:
Neck stiffness
Shoulder pain
Pain while turning the head
Difficulty raising the arm
Upper-back discomfort
Muscle tightness
Headaches associated with neck problems
Pain while working at a desk
Pain during exercise or sports
Reduced shoulder or neck movement
Tingling or numbness in the arm
The symptoms can vary from person to person. This is why treatment should not simply focus on reducing pain. A proper assessment can help identify what may be contributing to the problem.
How Physiotherapy Can Help With Neck and Shoulder Pain
Physiotherapy can help address pain, stiffness, weakness, movement problems, and reduced function.
Depending on the individual’s condition, a physiotherapist may use a combination of:
Movement assessment
Mobility exercises
Strength exercises
Posture and movement correction
Manual therapy when appropriate
Progressive rehabilitation
Exercise education
Activity modification
The aim is to help you move better, build appropriate strength, and gradually return to your normal activities.
Why Assessment Matters
Two people can have similar neck or shoulder pain but completely different causes.

For example, one person may have pain related to prolonged sitting, while another may develop symptoms after a gym or sports injury. Treating both people in exactly the same way may not be appropriate.
A detailed Bio-Mechanical Assessment can help evaluate how your body moves and identify movement or strength-related factors that may be contributing to your symptoms.
This type of assessment can be particularly useful for people who experience recurring pain during work, exercise, running, gym training, or sports.
Neck and Shoulder Pain in Athletes

Athletes and active individuals place different demands on their bodies. Repeated overhead movements, lifting, throwing, contact sports, and gym training can increase stress on the neck and shoulder region.
For an athlete, simply getting rid of pain may not be enough. The goal may also include improving strength, movement quality, control, and sports-specific performance.
Once the basic symptoms are under control, a structured High Performance Training programme can help active individuals work towards their performance goals.
Physiotherapy After a Sports Injury
Neck and shoulder symptoms can sometimes occur after a sports injury, fall, collision, or sudden movement.
A structured rehabilitation programme can help an individual progressively work on mobility, strength, balance, coordination, and function.
At Threads Physio, Sports Injury Rehabilitation includes assessment and progressive training designed around the individual’s injury and activity requirements.
Sports rehabilitation may involve testing areas such as strength, balance, speed, agility, endurance, and movement, depending on the individual’s needs.
Can Physiotherapy Be Done Online?
For certain conditions, follow-up sessions and exercise guidance may be possible through Online Physiotherapy.
Online physiotherapy can be useful for people who are unable to visit the clinic regularly or who need professional guidance with their rehabilitation exercises.
However, whether online physiotherapy is suitable depends on the individual’s symptoms and assessment requirements.
When Should You See a Physiotherapist?
Consider getting professional assessment if:
Your neck or shoulder pain keeps coming back
Pain is affecting your work or sleep
You have difficulty moving your neck or shoulder
Exercise is becoming difficult because of pain
Your symptoms started after an injury
You have weakness or reduced function
Home exercises have not helped
You want to safely return to sports or training
If symptoms include significant numbness, weakness, severe pain after an injury, or other concerning symptoms, medical assessment may be appropriate before beginning exercise-based rehabilitation.
Don’t Ignore Recurring Neck and Shoulder Pain
Neck and shoulder pain can sometimes become a recurring problem when the underlying movement, strength, workload, or activity-related factors are not addressed.
A personalised physiotherapy programme can help you understand your condition and work progressively towards better movement and function.
Whether your pain is related to your desk job, exercise, sports, or an old injury, the first step is understanding why the pain is happening and what your body needs to recover.

blocks.x: Knee pain can slowly become a part of everyday life. Climbing stairs, walking for long periods, exercising, or even getting up from a chair can become difficult. For people with knee osteoarthritis, the pain may continue despite medicines, physiotherapy, injections, and lifestyle changes.
When knee arthritis becomes advanced, many patients are advised to consider knee replacement surgery. But is surgery always the first or only option?
For selected patients, stem cell therapy for knee osteoarthritis may be an option worth discussing with an experienced orthopaedic specialist.

At Threads Physio, regenerative orthopaedic care includes bone marrow-derived stem cell therapy and adipocyte-derived cell-based treatment for selected cases of knee osteoarthritis. The treatment approach is based on the patient’s symptoms, clinical examination and MRI findings.
What Is Stem Cell Therapy for Knee Arthritis?
Stem cell therapy is a type of regenerative treatment that uses cells obtained from the patient’s own body.

In the approach used at Threads Physio, cells may be obtained from bone marrow or adipose (fat) tissue. Bone marrow aspirate can be processed to concentrate cells and growth factors before being delivered to the affected area.
For certain patients with knee osteoarthritis, the treatment focuses on the subchondral bone, which is the bone located underneath the cartilage.
The aim is to support the joint environment, reduce pain and improve function while potentially delaying the need for knee replacement in appropriate patients.
Why Is the Subchondral Bone Important?
Knee osteoarthritis is not only a problem involving cartilage.
Changes can also occur in the bone beneath the cartilage. These changes may include bone marrow lesions, inflammation and small structural changes that can contribute to knee pain.
This is why some regenerative treatment approaches focus on the bone beneath the damaged cartilage, rather than treating only the joint space.
The exact treatment approach depends on the patient’s MRI findings and overall condition.
How Does the Stem Cell Procedure Work?
A typical procedure may involve several steps:
1. Assessment and MRI Review
Before treatment, your doctor reviews your symptoms, medical history and MRI to determine whether you may be a suitable candidate.
2. Cell Harvesting
Bone marrow may be collected from the pelvic bone under local anaesthesia. In selected cases, adipose tissue may also be used.
3. Cell Preparation
The collected material is processed to concentrate the relevant cells and growth factors.
4. Targeted Injection
The prepared cell-based product is injected into the targeted area using image guidance.
5. Rehabilitation
After the procedure, a structured recovery and physiotherapy programme can help restore movement, strength and function.
At Threads Physio, rehabilitation is incorporated into the treatment pathway following the procedure.
Who May Be a Candidate for Stem Cell Therapy?
Stem cell treatment is not suitable for everyone with knee pain.
A detailed assessment is important. Some patients with knee osteoarthritis, particularly those with specific changes visible on MRI, may be considered for treatment.
Potential candidates may include people who:
Have symptomatic knee osteoarthritis
Have subchondral bone changes visible on MRI
Continue to experience pain despite conservative treatment
Have tried options such as physiotherapy or injections without adequate improvement
Want to explore joint-preservation options before considering knee replacement
Are medically suitable for the procedure
On the other hand, patients with severe joint deformity, active infection or certain medical conditions may not be suitable.
Your MRI and clinical assessment are therefore important before making a treatment decision.
Can Stem Cell Therapy Help You Avoid Knee Replacement?
This is one of the most common questions patients ask.
The answer depends on the individual patient.

Published research on bone-marrow-derived cell treatment for knee osteoarthritis has reported long-term outcomes, including studies examining whether treatment can delay or avoid knee replacement in selected patients. However, individual results can vary depending on factors such as the severity of arthritis, bone changes, age, activity level and overall health.
Therefore, stem cell therapy should not be presented as a guaranteed replacement for knee surgery.
Instead, it can be considered as a joint-preservation option for appropriately selected patients.
Stem Cell Therapy vs Knee Replacement
Knee replacement is a well-established treatment for advanced knee arthritis. However, it is a major surgical procedure and involves a significant rehabilitation period.
Stem cell therapy is different because it aims to preserve the patient’s natural knee rather than replace the joint.
The right option depends on the patient’s condition. A specialist assessment is essential before deciding between treatment options.

Because the treatment uses cells obtained from the patient’s own body in the described protocols, there is no donor-related immune rejection issue.
However, no medical procedure is completely risk-free.
A proper consultation is important to understand whether you are medically suitable and what potential risks and benefits apply to your specific case.
Why MRI Is Important Before Treatment
An MRI can provide important information about the condition of the knee, including cartilage damage and changes in the underlying bone.
This information can help the orthopaedic specialist determine whether regenerative treatment may be appropriate.
If you have already been advised to undergo knee replacement, getting an expert review of your MRI may help you understand whether a joint-preservation option is worth considering.

Frequently Asked Questions

It is a regenerative treatment approach that uses cells obtained from sources such as bone marrow or adipose tissue. In selected patients, the cells are processed and delivered to targeted areas of the knee.

Neck and shoulder pain are increasingly common problems affecting people of all ages. Long hours at a desk, poor posture, excessive smartphone use, repetitive movements, sports activities, and muscle strain can all contribute to discomfort and restricted movement.

While occasional stiffness may improve with rest, persistent or recurring neck and shoulder pain can interfere with work, exercise, sleep, and everyday activities. Physiotherapy can help identify the underlying cause of your pain and develop a personalised treatment plan to improve mobility, strength, and function.
What Causes Neck and Shoulder Pain?
Neck and shoulder discomfort can develop due to several factors, including:
Poor sitting or standing posture
Prolonged computer or mobile-phone use
Muscle tightness and weakness
Cervical spine problems
Rotator cuff injuries
Sports-related injuries
Repetitive movements
Muscle strains and sprains
Stress-related muscle tension
Previous injuries
Lack of physical activity
Athletes and active individuals may also experience neck or shoulder pain because of overtraining, improper technique, inadequate recovery, or muscle imbalance.
Common Symptoms
Depending on the underlying problem, symptoms may include:
Neck stiffness
Shoulder pain or aching
Reduced range of motion
Muscle tightness
Pain while turning the head
Pain when lifting the arm
Headaches associated with neck tension
Shoulder weakness
Pain extending toward the upper back or arm
Tingling or numbness in some cases
If symptoms are persistent, worsening, or associated with significant weakness, numbness, or other neurological symptoms, professional assessment is recommended.
How Can Physiotherapy Help With Neck and Shoulder Pain?
Physiotherapy focuses on identifying the factors contributing to your pain rather than simply treating the symptoms.
A physiotherapist may assess your posture, joint mobility, muscle strength, movement patterns, and functional limitations before designing an individualised treatment programme.
Treatment may include:
1. Manual Therapy
Hands-on techniques can help improve joint mobility, reduce muscle stiffness, and support normal movement.
2. Therapeutic Exercises
Specific exercises can strengthen the neck, shoulder, upper-back, and core muscles. A structured exercise programme can also help improve posture and movement control.
3. Posture Correction
Poor posture can place additional stress on the neck and shoulder muscles. Physiotherapy can teach you practical strategies for improving your sitting, standing, and working positions.
4. Mobility and Stretching
Targeted mobility exercises and stretches may help improve flexibility and reduce stiffness around the neck, shoulders, and upper back.
5. Sports Rehabilitation

For athletes, returning to activity too quickly after an injury can increase the risk of recurrence. A progressive rehabilitation programme can help restore strength, mobility, coordination, and confidence before returning to sport.
Explore Sports Injury Rehabilitation for specialised rehabilitation support.
Physiotherapy for Desk-Related Neck and Shoulder Pain
People who spend several hours working at a computer are particularly susceptible to neck and shoulder discomfort.
A poorly positioned monitor, prolonged sitting, unsupported arms, or frequent smartphone use can contribute to muscle fatigue and stiffness.
Simple strategies such as adjusting your workstation, taking regular movement breaks, maintaining an appropriate screen height, and performing prescribed exercises can make a significant difference.
Physiotherapy can also help identify movement and posture habits that may be contributing to recurring symptoms.
Neck and Shoulder Pain in Athletes
Athletes may develop neck and shoulder pain because of repetitive overhead movements, contact injuries, training errors, poor technique, or insufficient recovery.
Rehabilitation should address more than pain reduction. The goal is to restore strength, mobility, stability, coordination, and sport-specific performance.
For active individuals looking to improve physical capacity and reduce injury risk, High Performance Training can complement rehabilitation and conditioning.
Can Online Physiotherapy Help?

Not every physiotherapy session requires an in-person visit. Depending on the condition, symptoms, and treatment requirements, online physiotherapy can provide assessment, exercise guidance, education, and rehabilitation support remotely.
It can be particularly useful for people who have difficulty travelling to a clinic or need ongoing guidance between appointments.
Learn more about Online Physiotherapy.
When Should You See a Physiotherapist?
Consider consulting a physiotherapist if:
Neck or shoulder pain continues for several days or weeks
Pain repeatedly returns
You have difficulty moving your neck or shoulder
Pain is affecting your work, sleep, or exercise
You have weakness or reduced function
You are recovering from a sports injury
You want to safely return to physical activity
Early assessment can help identify contributing factors and prevent a minor movement problem from becoming a persistent issue.
How to Prevent Neck and Shoulder Pain
A few practical habits can support neck and shoulder health:
Maintain good posture while working
Adjust your workstation ergonomically
Take movement breaks during prolonged sitting
Avoid staying in one position for extended periods
Strengthen the upper back and shoulder muscles
Maintain regular physical activity
Warm up before sports and workouts
Progress exercise intensity gradually
Prioritise recovery after demanding physical activity
Why Choose Physiotherapy for Neck and Shoulder Pain?

Physiotherapy provides a structured approach to managing musculoskeletal pain. Instead of relying solely on temporary symptom relief, treatment can focus on improving movement quality, strength, flexibility, posture, and physical function.
A personalised rehabilitation programme can also help you understand what may be contributing to your symptoms and how to manage them in the long term.

Don’t let persistent neck or shoulder pain limit your work, exercise, or everyday life. A professional physiotherapy assessment can help determine the likely cause of your symptoms and identify an appropriate treatment and rehabilitation approach.

blocks.x: Pushups are one of the most effective bodyweight exercises for building strength in the chest, shoulders, arms and core. However, if you experience shoulder pain after pushups, it may be a sign that your technique, training volume, mobility or shoulder strength needs attention.

A mild muscle ache after exercise can be normal, but sharp, persistent or recurring shoulder pain should not be ignored. Poor pushup mechanics and excessive training can place unnecessary stress on the shoulder joint and surrounding tendons.

At Threads Physio, shoulder conditions are assessed through an individualized approach that may include physiotherapy, therapeutic exercise, manual therapy, mobility work and sports-specific rehabilitation.
Why Does My Shoulder Hurt After Pushups?

The shoulder is a highly mobile joint that relies on coordinated movement between the joint, rotator cuff, shoulder blade and surrounding muscles. During a pushup, the shoulder has to support a significant portion of your body weight.
Several factors can contribute to shoulder pain after pushups:
1. Incorrect Pushup Form
One of the most common problems is allowing the elbows to flare excessively outward.

When the elbows move too far away from the body, the shoulder may experience increased stress. A more controlled position, generally with the elbows moving at approximately a 45-degree angle from the torso, can help improve shoulder mechanics.
Your hands should generally be positioned around shoulder width, while your core remains engaged throughout the movement.
2. Weak Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Stabilizers
Your chest and arm muscles may become stronger faster than the smaller muscles responsible for stabilizing the shoulder.
The rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers help control shoulder movement. If these muscles are weak or poorly coordinated, repetitive pushups may contribute to discomfort, fatigue or irritation.
3. Increasing Exercise Volume Too Quickly
Going from a small number of pushups to dozens of repetitions in a short period can overload muscles and tendons.
Training progression should be gradual. Increasing repetitions, frequency and intensity simultaneously can increase the risk of overuse-related pain.
4. Limited Shoulder or Upper-Body Mobility
Restricted shoulder, thoracic spine or chest mobility can affect your pushup technique.
If you cannot comfortably move your shoulder through its required range, your body may compensate by changing the position of the shoulder blade or upper arm.
5. Previous Shoulder Injury
A previous rotator cuff injury, instability, tendinitis, bursitis or other shoulder problem may make pushups uncomfortable.
If shoulder pain repeatedly returns whenever you resume exercise, it is worth having the underlying movement pattern and shoulder function assessed.
Is Shoulder Pain After Pushups Normal?
Not every ache means you have sustained a serious injury.
Normal post-exercise soreness
Delayed-onset muscle soreness, or DOMS, typically develops after exercise and may feel like a generalized muscle ache or stiffness.
Pain that needs attention

Sharp, stabbing, pinching or persistent pain during a pushup is different. Pain accompanied by weakness, swelling, restricted movement, numbness or pain at rest should be evaluated by a qualified healthcare professional.
The existing Threads Physio guidance similarly recommends stopping exercise when pain is sharp rather than attempting to push through it.
How to Correct Your Pushup Technique
Good technique can reduce unnecessary stress on the shoulder.
Keep Your Elbows Controlled
Avoid allowing the elbows to flare completely sideways. Keep them in a more controlled position as you lower and push your body upward.
Position Your Hands Correctly
Place your hands approximately beneath or slightly outside your shoulders rather than excessively wide or far forward.
Maintain a Neutral Spine
Keep your head, upper back, hips and legs aligned. Avoid allowing your hips to sag or your lower back to excessively arch.
Control the Movement
Avoid dropping quickly toward the floor. Lower your body under control and push back up while maintaining consistent shoulder-blade and trunk control.
What Should You Do If Your Shoulder Hurts After Pushups?
If pushups are causing pain, temporarily reduce or stop the painful movement rather than repeatedly testing the shoulder.
You can consider:
Reducing pushup repetitions
Using wall pushups as a regression
Trying an incline pushup
Working on shoulder and thoracic mobility
Strengthening the rotator cuff and scapular muscles
Returning gradually once pain has settled
Getting a professional assessment if symptoms persist
The goal is not simply to eliminate pain temporarily but to identify why the shoulder is being overloaded.
Shoulder Pain Treatment: What Can Physiotherapy Include?
The appropriate Shoulder Pain Treatment depends on the underlying cause.
A physiotherapy assessment can examine shoulder range of motion, strength, posture, movement patterns and the activities that reproduce your symptoms.
Depending on the assessment, treatment may include:
Manual therapy and joint mobilization
Therapeutic exercises
Rotator cuff strengthening
Scapular stabilization exercises
Mobility exercises
Postural correction
Activity modification
Gradual return-to-exercise programming
Sports-specific rehabilitation

Threads Physio describes its shoulder rehabilitation approach as individualized, with assessment followed by targeted pain-management techniques, manual therapy, therapeutic exercise and sports-specific rehabilitation where appropriate.
Can Acupuncture Treatment Help Shoulder Pain?
For some patients, Acupuncture Treatment may be considered as part of a broader physiotherapy and pain-management plan.

Acupuncture may be used alongside rehabilitation strategies to help manage musculoskeletal pain and support movement during recovery. However, it should not replace assessment of the underlying cause of persistent shoulder pain.
At Threads Physio, acupuncture therapy is offered as one of the available treatment approaches.
Shoulder Pain and Sports Injury Rehabilitation
If you regularly participate in the gym, running, cricket, badminton, tennis or other sports, shoulder pain can interfere with training and performance.
Sports Injury Rehabilitation focuses on helping you safely progress from pain management to strength, movement control and sport-specific activity.
Rather than immediately returning to your previous workout volume, rehabilitation may involve progressive loading and movement retraining.

The objective is to restore confidence and function while reducing the likelihood of recurring symptoms. Threads Physio specifically provides sports injury rehabilitation and sports-specific rehabilitation services.
When Should You See a Physiotherapist?
Consider professional assessment if:
Shoulder pain continues for several days
Pain repeatedly returns during pushups or workouts
You have difficulty lifting your arm
Your shoulder feels weak or unstable
You experience clicking or painful popping
You have swelling or significant tenderness
Pain interferes with sleep
You experience tingling or numbness
Pain started after a fall or sudden injury
Your shoulder pain is getting worse with exercise

Persistent symptoms should not simply be treated by repeatedly resting and restarting the same exercise. A proper assessment can help determine whether the problem is related to muscle weakness, mobility restrictions, tendon irritation, joint dysfunction or another condition. Threads Physio lists persistent pain, limited range of motion, weakness, swelling, trauma and activity-related worsening among signs that warrant professional assessment.
How to Prevent Shoulder Pain During Pushups
Prevention starts with appropriate exercise progression and good movement quality.
Warm Up Before Training
Perform gentle shoulder, arm and upper-back movements before starting your workout.
Strengthen the Shoulder
Include exercises targeting the rotator cuff, scapular stabilizers and upper back.
Improve Mobility
Address restrictions in the chest, thoracic spine and shoulder when appropriate.
Progress Gradually
Increase repetitions and training volume progressively instead of making sudden jumps.
Listen to Pain Signals
Muscle fatigue is different from sharp or escalating joint pain. Do not repeatedly exercise through significant pain.
Final Takeaway
Shoulder pain after pushups is often related to technique, excessive training volume, inadequate strength or mobility, but persistent symptoms can have other causes.

Improving pushup mechanics, modifying your training and progressively strengthening the shoulder may help. If pain continues, recurs or affects your daily activities, professional evaluation is recommended.

blocks.x: Arthroscopy has transformed the way many joint and sports-related conditions are diagnosed and treated. With minimally invasive techniques, orthopedic surgeons can evaluate and treat problems affecting joints such as the knee, shoulder, ankle, hip, and elbow through small incisions.

However, successful arthroscopic treatment is not only about the procedure itself. Post-operative physiotherapy and structured rehabilitation play an equally important role in helping patients regain mobility, strength, stability, and confidence.

For healthcare professionals interested in sports medicine and rehabilitation, understanding the relationship between arthroscopy and physiotherapy can provide valuable clinical knowledge and improve patient outcomes.
What Is Arthroscopy?
Arthroscopy is a minimally invasive orthopedic procedure that allows a surgeon to examine the inside of a joint using a small camera called an arthroscope.

The arthroscope is inserted through a small incision, and additional small instruments may be used when treatment is required. Depending on the condition, arthroscopic procedures can be used to address problems such as:
Meniscus injuries
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries
Cartilage damage
Shoulder instability
Rotator cuff-related conditions
Joint inflammation
Certain sports-related injuries

Compared with some traditional open procedures, arthroscopy generally involves smaller incisions and may allow a more targeted approach to joint treatment. The appropriate procedure and recovery plan, however, depend on the patient’s diagnosis, surgical findings, and overall health.
Why Is Physiotherapy Important After Arthroscopy?
An arthroscopic procedure can address the underlying structural problem, but the body still needs time and appropriate rehabilitation to recover.
After surgery, patients may experience:
Pain and swelling
Reduced range of motion
Muscle weakness
Reduced joint stability
Difficulty performing everyday movements
Reduced confidence when putting weight on or using the affected joint
A properly designed physiotherapy programme helps address these challenges progressively.
1. Restoring Range of Motion
Following surgery, stiffness can restrict normal joint movement. Physiotherapy may include carefully selected mobility and flexibility exercises to gradually restore the appropriate range of motion.
2. Rebuilding Muscle Strength
Reduced activity after surgery can contribute to muscle weakness. Progressive strengthening exercises can help restore muscle function and support the affected joint.
For example, after certain knee procedures, rehabilitation may focus on rebuilding quadriceps and hamstring strength while progressing according to the patient’s surgical protocol.
3. Improving Balance and Joint Stability
For athletes and active individuals, strength alone is not enough. Rehabilitation may also include balance, coordination, proprioception, and neuromuscular exercises.
These components can be particularly important when preparing a patient to return to sports or physically demanding activities.
4. Supporting a Safe Return to Activity

Returning to normal activities too quickly may increase the risk of setbacks. Physiotherapists work with patients to progress rehabilitation according to functional milestones rather than simply relying on the number of days or weeks since surgery.
The rehabilitation programme should be individualized according to the procedure performed, healing progress, symptoms, strength, mobility, and the patient’s goals.
Arthroscopy and Sports Medicine: Why Rehabilitation Matters
Sports medicine involves more than treating an injury. The broader goal is to help an athlete return to appropriate levels of physical activity safely and effectively.
This makes collaboration between orthopedic surgeons, physiotherapists, sports medicine specialists, and other healthcare professionals particularly valuable.
An athlete recovering from an ACL reconstruction, for example, may require a rehabilitation programme involving:
Early rehabilitation → Mobility → Strength → Neuromuscular control → Functional training → Sport-specific conditioning → Return-to-sport assessment
Each stage should be progressed according to clinical assessment and the individual’s recovery.
The Growing Importance of Physiotherapy Education

As minimally invasive orthopedic procedures and sports medicine continue to evolve, physiotherapists need a strong understanding of musculoskeletal conditions, rehabilitation principles, exercise prescription, and post-operative care.
Specialized education can help healthcare professionals strengthen their understanding of:
Orthopedic rehabilitation
Sports injuries
Post-operative physiotherapy
Exercise therapy
Functional assessment
Injury prevention
Sports-specific rehabilitation
Patient-centered recovery planning

For professionals looking to develop their expertise, structured programmes such as the Fellowship in Physiotherapy can provide an opportunity to build knowledge relevant to modern orthopedic and sports rehabilitation.
Learning From Experienced Orthopedic Specialists
Exposure to experienced clinicians can be particularly valuable for healthcare professionals who want to understand how surgical treatment and rehabilitation work together.
Dr. Manu Bora is associated with Arthroscopy College and its focus on arthroscopy, sports medicine, and orthopedic education.

Learning from experienced specialists can help professionals develop a broader perspective on patient management—from understanding the underlying injury and surgical procedure to appreciating the rehabilitation requirements that follow.
Arthroscopy Is Only One Part of the Recovery Journey
One of the most important principles in orthopedic care is that surgery and rehabilitation should not be viewed as completely separate stages.
A successful recovery often involves a continuum:
Accurate diagnosis → Appropriate treatment → Post-operative protection → Physiotherapy → Progressive strengthening → Functional recovery → Return to activity

The exact pathway differs from patient to patient. A person undergoing arthroscopy for a meniscus injury may have very different rehabilitation requirements from someone recovering from ACL reconstruction or shoulder surgery.
Therefore, rehabilitation should always be individualized and guided by the treating medical and physiotherapy team.
How Can Aspiring Physiotherapists Build Their Expertise?
Physiotherapists who want to work in orthopedics and sports medicine can benefit from combining theoretical knowledge with practical clinical exposure.
A specialized fellowship can be useful for professionals who want to deepen their understanding of musculoskeletal rehabilitation and develop skills relevant to real-world clinical practice.
The Arthroscopy College Fellowship in Physiotherapy is designed for professionals interested in expanding their knowledge in this area.
Final Thoughts
Arthroscopy has become an important component of modern orthopedic and sports medicine. But treating the joint is only one part of the patient’s recovery journey.
Physiotherapy helps bridge the gap between surgical treatment and functional recovery.

Through progressive rehabilitation, appropriate exercise, strength development, mobility training, and functional assessment, patients can work toward regaining their physical capabilities under professional guidance.

For physiotherapists and healthcare professionals interested in orthopedic and sports rehabilitation, developing specialized knowledge in arthroscopy-related care can be an important step toward advancing their clinical expertise.

blocks.x: The meniscus plays a critical role in knee joint stability, load distribution, shock absorption and cartilage protection. As arthroscopic surgery continues to evolve, the management of meniscal injuries has increasingly moved toward meniscus preservation and repair whenever clinically appropriate, rather than routinely removing damaged tissue.

For orthopedic surgeons, developing advanced meniscus repair skills is therefore an important component of modern knee arthroscopy training. Treating a meniscal tear requires more than identifying the injury. Surgeons must understand the tear pattern, tissue quality, vascularity, location and stability of the tear before deciding whether repair is appropriate.

A structured hands-on meniscus repair course can help surgeons develop these technical and decision-making skills through practical training, surgical models, case discussions and supervised operating-room exposure. Arthroscopy College’s fellowship curriculum, for example, specifically includes meniscus repair alongside ACL/PCL reconstruction, cartilage procedures and other sports-medicine surgeries.
What Is Meniscus Repair?
Meniscus repair is an arthroscopic procedure designed to preserve and stabilize a torn meniscus rather than removing the damaged portion unnecessarily.
Depending on the tear characteristics, surgeons may use different repair strategies, including:
Inside-out repair
Outside-in repair
All-inside repair
Different meniscal suture configurations
Repair devices and implants selected according to the tear pattern
The choice of technique depends on factors such as tear location, morphology, tissue quality, vascular supply and associated injuries.
For surgeons learning knee arthroscopy, understanding when to repair, how to repair and when partial meniscectomy may be more appropriate is an important part of developing sound clinical judgment.
Why Meniscus Preservation Is Important
The meniscus contributes to several important functions within the knee. It helps distribute loads across the joint, contributes to stability and provides protection to the articular cartilage.
When a tear is repairable, preserving the meniscal tissue can be an important consideration in long-term joint preservation.
This is why modern arthroscopy training increasingly emphasizes meniscus repair and preservation techniques, rather than focusing exclusively on meniscectomy.
A surgeon therefore needs to evaluate each tear individually and understand the biological and mechanical factors that influence healing.
The Importance of Hands-On Meniscus Repair Training

Reading textbooks and watching surgical videos can provide a strong theoretical foundation, but arthroscopic surgery also requires three-dimensional orientation, instrument control, triangulation, tissue handling and precise suturing.
These skills improve through deliberate practical training.
A hands-on arthroscopy program can expose surgeons to:
Arthroscopic Orientation : Understanding portals, camera positioning and instrument handling is fundamental to knee arthroscopy.
Meniscal Tear Assessment : Surgeons need to systematically evaluate the meniscus and identify different tear patterns before selecting a treatment strategy.
Suture Techniques : Practical training allows surgeons to understand different suture configurations and their application to specific tear patterns.
Implant Selection : Different tears may require different repair devices or fixation strategies. Learning how to select an appropriate implant is an important part of procedural training.
Surgical Decision-Making : The objective is not simply to learn a technique but to understand which technique should be used, when and why.
Meniscus Repair Techniques Every Orthopedic Surgeon Should Understand
A comprehensive meniscus repair training program should introduce surgeons to multiple approaches rather than relying on a single technique.
Inside-Out Meniscus Repair

Inside-out repair has traditionally been an important technique for treating certain meniscal tears. It can provide strong fixation but requires careful attention to surrounding neurovascular structures.
Outside-In Meniscus Repair
Outside-in techniques can be useful for selected tears, particularly in certain locations of the meniscus. Proper portal placement and needle trajectory are essential.
All-Inside Meniscus Repair

All-inside techniques use specialized devices to place fixation entirely within the joint. They can offer procedural efficiency but require familiarity with implant deployment and appropriate positioning.
The choice between techniques should be based on the individual tear rather than applying one repair method universally.
Meniscus Repair and ACL Reconstruction
Meniscal injuries frequently occur alongside ligament injuries, particularly ACL injuries.
This makes meniscus management an important component of comprehensive sports-medicine and knee arthroscopy training.
When an ACL injury is accompanied by a repairable meniscal tear, the surgeon must evaluate both pathologies and develop an appropriate surgical plan.

For orthopedic surgeons pursuing advanced arthroscopy training, learning ACL reconstruction and meniscus repair together can therefore provide a more complete understanding of sports-related knee surgery.
Arthroscopy College’s fellowship curriculum includes both ACL/PCL reconstruction with internal brace techniques and meniscus repair.
Conclusion

Meniscus repair is an important skill for orthopedic surgeons developing expertise in modern knee arthroscopy. As the emphasis on meniscal preservation and joint preservation continues, surgeons need to understand not only the technical aspects of repair but also patient selection, tear assessment and procedure-specific decision-making.
A structured hands-on meniscus repair course can provide an opportunity to develop these skills through practical training, case discussions, simulation and supervised surgical exposure.
For orthopedic surgeons looking to expand their sports-medicine expertise, meniscus repair should be considered an essential component of comprehensive arthroscopy fellowship training in India.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is meniscus repair training? Meniscus repair training teaches orthopedic surgeons how to assess meniscal tears, select appropriate repair strategies and perform arthroscopic suturing techniques.

Which meniscus repair techniques should surgeons learn? Training may include inside-out, outside-in and all-inside repair techniques, along with different suture configurations and implant-selection principles.

Why is hands-on training important for meniscus repair? Arthroscopy requires technical skills such as triangulation, instrument handling and precise suturing that are difficult to develop through theory alone.

Can meniscus repair be performed along with ACL reconstruction? Yes. Meniscal tears can occur alongside ACL injuries, making combined assessment and management an important part of sports-medicine practice.

Is meniscus repair included in Arthroscopy College’s fellowship? Yes. The current fellowship curriculum listed by Arthroscopy College includes meniscus repair along with ACL/PCL reconstruction, cartilage transplantation, ligament repair and shoulder procedures.

Who can join an arthroscopy fellowship? Arthroscopy College states that its fellowship is intended for young orthopedic surgeons and practicing surgeons who want additional training in knee, shoulder and ankle arthroscopy.

At Threads Physio, we help people fix shoulder pain every single day. The good news is: most of the time, it is fixable without surgery.
This guide will tell you exactly why left hand shoulder pain happens, how to stop it, and when you should call a doctor.
1. Is It Serious? (Check This First)
Before we talk about muscles and bones, we must be safe. Sometimes, pain in the left arm or shoulder can be a warning sign from your heart.
Call a doctor immediately if you have shoulder pain AND any of these:
Chest pain or pressure (like an elephant sitting on your chest).
Trouble breathing.
Sweating a lot (cold sweat).

If you only have shoulder pain and you feel fine otherwise, it is likely a muscle or joint problem. Let’s look at the most common reasons.
3. How to Fix It (Simple Treatments)
You don’t always need medicine. Try these simple steps at home first.
The R.I.C.E Method: * Rest: Stop doing the thing that hurts.
Ice: Put an ice pack on it for 15 minutes (great for new injuries).
Compression: Use a light bandage if it’s swollen.
Elevation: Keep it comfortable.
Sleep Right: Don’t sleep on your sore left side. Try sleeping on your back with a pillow under your left arm.
Gentle Stretches: Moving a little bit helps blood flow to the area.
4. Physiotherapy: The Magic Fix
If your pain lasts more than 3 days, pills won’t fix the root cause. You need to fix the movement.
At Threads Physio, we use special techniques to stop the pain and make your shoulder strong again. We help with:

6. Prevention: Keep Your Shoulders Happy Once the pain is gone, let’s keep it away!
Fix Your Desk: Keep your computer screen at eye level so you don’t look down.

7. People Also Ask (FAQs)
Q: Can gas cause left shoulder pain?
A: Yes! oddly enough, trapped gas usually affects the belly, but sometimes the pain can travel up to the shoulder. This is called “referred pain.”
Q: Why does my left arm hurt at night?
A: This is very common with Rotator Cuff injuries or Frozen Shoulder. Lying flat changes the blood flow and gravity pulling on the joint.
Q: How do I know if it is muscle or bone pain?
A: Muscle pain usually feels “tight” or “burning.” Bone pain feels “deep” and “boring” (like a toothache in your arm).

blocks.x: Imagine this: You had a long day. You are tired. You crawl into bed, ready for a good night’s sleep. But just as you drift off… OUCH. A sharp pain in your shoulder wakes you up.
Sound familiar?
You are not alone. Millions of people suffer from shoulder pain while sleeping. It is one of the most common reasons people visit a physiotherapist. The good news? You don’t have to live with it.

At Threads Physio, we help people just like you get back to a pain-free life. In this guide, we will explain why your shoulder hurts at night, how to fix your sleeping position, and the best exercises to stop the pain for good.
Why Does My Shoulder Hurt More at Night?
Have you ever wondered why your shoulder feels okay during the day but throbs at night?
It’s not just in your head. Here is the simple science:
Gravity: When you stand, gravity pulls your arm down. This opens up space in your shoulder joint. When you lie down, that space gets smaller, and things can get “pinched.”
Blood Flow: When you stay still for a long time (like sleeping), blood flow slows down. This can make inflammation (swelling) worse.
Pressure: If you sleep on your side, you are squishing your shoulder joint with your whole body weight.
Expert Note: Night pain is often a “Red Flag” (a warning sign) that your shoulder needs attention. Don’t ignore it!
Top 5 Common Causes of Shoulder Pain
If your shoulder wakes you up, it is usually because of one of these 5 reasons.
1. Rotator Cuff Injury

Think of your shoulder like a sleeve. The rotator cuff is a group of muscles and tendons that hold your arm in place. If these tendons get tiny tears or get swollen (Tendinitis), lying on them hurts a lot.
Signs: Pain when lifting your arm, weakness, and dull ache at night.
2. Shoulder Bursitis
Inside your shoulder, there are tiny fluid-filled sacs called “bursae.” They act like small cushions. If they get swollen, it is called Bursitis.
Signs: Hot or burning feeling, pain when lying on the side.
3. Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis)
This is exactly what it sounds like. Your shoulder joint gets stiff and “frozen.” It happens slowly and can take months to heal without help.
Signs: Severe stiffness, you can’t move your arm far, and deep pain at night.
4. Shoulder Impingement
This happens when the bones in your shoulder rub against the tendons. It’s like a rope fraying on a sharp rock.
Signs: Sharp pinch when you reach up or reach behind your back.
5. Neck Problems (Referred Pain)
Sometimes, your shoulder is fine! The problem might be in your neck. A pinched nerve in your neck can send pain signals down to your shoulder.
Signs: Pain travels from your neck down to your arm; tingling or numbness.
Is Your Sleeping Position Hurting You?
Your favorite way to sleep might be the villain. Let’s look at the “Good,” the “Bad,” and the “Ugly” positions.
The BAD Position: Sleeping on the Painful Side
This puts direct pressure on the sore spot. It cuts off blood flow and squishes the inflamed tissues. Avoid this if possible!
The UGLY Position: Sleeping on Your Stomach
Sleeping on your stomach forces your neck to twist and your shoulders to hunch forward. This is terrible for your spine and shoulders.
The GOOD Position: Back Sleeping
Sleeping on your back is the safest choice. It keeps your spine straight and takes pressure off your shoulders.
Pro Tip: Put a small pillow under your painful arm for extra support.
The “Side Sleeper” Hack (The Quarter Turn)
Can’t sleep on your back? Try the Quarter Turn:
Lie on your good side.
Place a thick pillow in front of your chest.
Rest your painful arm on the pillow (like you are hugging it). This keeps your shoulder “open” and stops it from drooping.
7 Simple Exercises to Stop the Pain (Do These Tonight!)
Before you go to bed, try these simple movements to loosen up your stiff joints.
1. Pendulum Swing

blocks.x: Have you ever woken up with a neck so stiff you couldn’t turn your head? Or felt a burning, nagging pain in your shoulders after a long day at school or sitting at a computer?

You are not alone. In fact, neck and shoulder pain is one of the most common reasons people visit a doctor today. It can make simple things—like carrying a backpack, sleeping, or even looking down at your phone—feel terrible.
The good news? You don’t have to live with it.

At Threads Physio, we specialize in fixing these problems without scary surgeries or endless painkillers. This guide will teach you exactly what causes this pain (hello, “Text Neck”!), when to see a specialist, and the best exercises to get you moving freely again.
What Causes Neck and Shoulder Pain?
Your neck and shoulders are like best friends—they work together. But because they move so much and hold up your heavy head (which weighs about 5kg, like a bowling ball!), they can get hurt easily.
Here are the most common reasons your neck and shoulders might hurt:
Bad Posture: Slouching in a chair or hunching over a desk makes your muscles work double-time to hold your head up.
Muscle Strain: This happens when you overuse your muscles, like carrying a heavy bag on one shoulder or playing sports without warming up.
Stress: When you are stressed, you naturally tighten your shoulders, pulling them up toward your ears. This causes tension headaches and pain.
Arthritis: As we get older, the joints in our neck can get a little “rusty” (wear and tear), causing pain and stiffness.
Pinched Nerves: Sometimes, a nerve gets squished by a bone or muscle, sending sharp “electric” pain down your arm.
Did you know? Your shoulder is the most flexible joint in your body, but that also makes it unstable and easy to injure!
The “Text Neck” Epidemic: Are You Guilty?
This is a huge problem for everyone today, from kids to adults. “Text Neck” is the pain you get from looking down at your phone or tablet for too long.
When your head is upright, it weighs about 5kg. But for every inch you tilt your head forward to look at a screen, the pressure on your neck doubles!
At 15 degrees: Your head feels like it weighs 12kg.
At 60 degrees (looking at a phone): Your head feels like it weighs 27kg! Imagine carrying an 8-year-old child around your neck all day. That is what your muscles are feeling.
If you spend hours on your phone, this is likely the #1 cause of your pain.
Symptoms: When Should You See a Physio?
Most neck pain goes away with rest. But sometimes, you need a professional Bio-Mechanical Assessment to find the root cause.
See a physio immediately if:
The pain spreads down your arms or legs.
You feel numbness, tingling, or weakness in your hands.
You have a fever or headache along with the neck pain.
The pain started after a fall or car accident.
The pain hasn’t gone away after a week of rest.
How Physiotherapy Helps (The Threads Physio Way)
At Threads Physio, we don’t just treat the pain; we treat the person. Here is how our specialists fix neck and shoulder issues:
1. Diagnosis
We start by listening to you. We look at how you sit, stand, and move. We check if your pain is coming from a muscle, a joint, or a nerve.
2. Manual Therapy
This is “hands-on” treatment. Our experts use special massage techniques and gentle movements to:
Relax tight muscles.
Unlock stiff joints.
Improve blood flow to heal the area faster.
3. Exercise Therapy

Weak muscles hurt. Strong muscles support. We design a custom plan to strengthen your upper back and neck so they can hold your head up effortlessly. (Check out our High Performance Training for advanced strengthening).
4. Posture Correction
We teach you how to sit and stand correctly so the pain doesn’t come back. This is crucial for students and office workers!
5. Electrotherapy
For acute pain, we might use safe technologies like Ultrasound or TENS (tiny electrical pulses) to block pain signals and reduce swelling.
Top 10 Exercises for Neck and Shoulder Pain Relief
Note: Always move slowly. If you feel sharp pain, STOP.
1. Shoulder Rolls (The Warm-Up)
Why: Loosens up the big muscles.
How: Stand tall. Lift your shoulders up to your ears, roll them back, and drop them down. Do this 10 times forward and 10 times backward.
2. Neck Tilts (Upper Trapezius Stretch)
Why: Relieves tension on the side of the neck.
How: Sit on one hand to anchor your shoulder down. Gently tilt your ear toward the opposite shoulder. You should feel a nice stretch. Hold for 20 seconds. Repeat on the other side.
3. Chin Tucks (The “Double Chin”)
Why: The #1 fix for Text Neck and Forward Head Posture.
How: Sit straight. Pull your chin straight back like you are making a “double chin” (don’t look up or down). Hold for 5 seconds. Repeat 10 times.
4. Corner Pec Stretch
Why: Opens up a tight chest caused by slouching.
How: Stand facing a corner of a room. Put your forearms on the walls (elbows at shoulder height). Lean into the corner until you feel a stretch in your chest. Hold for 30 seconds.
5. Scapular Squeezes (Shoulder Blade Squeeze)
Why: Strengthens the upper back.
How: Sit tall. Squeeze your shoulder blades together like you are trying to hold a pencil between them. Hold for 5 seconds. Do 10 reps.
6. Arm Circles
Why: improves mobility.
How: Stand with arms out to the side. Make small circles with your arms, gradually getting bigger. Do 10 circles forward and 10 backward.
7. Thread the Needle
Why: Great for twisting mobility in the upper back.
How: Start on all fours (hands and knees). Reach your right arm underneath your left arm and twist your body until your right shoulder touches the floor. Hold for a few seconds. Switch sides.
8. Wall Angels
Why: The ultimate posture test!

How: Stand with your back flat against a wall. Put your arms up like a “stick up” (elbows and wrists touching the wall). Slide your arms up and down without letting them leave the wall. It’s harder than it looks!
9. Child’s Pose
Why: Relaxes the whole back.
How: Kneel on the floor. Sit back on your heels and reach your arms forward on the floor. Rest your forehead on the ground. Breathe deeply.
10. Doorway Stretch
Why: Relieves tight shoulders.
How: Stand in a doorway. Hold the door frame with one hand at waist level. Turn your body away from that hand. Feel the stretch in the front of your shoulder.
Daily Habits to Prevent Pain
You can do exercises all day, but if you sleep wrong or sit wrong, the pain will return.
Sleep Right: Try to sleep on your back or side. Sleeping on your stomach twists your neck for hours!
Screen Height: Raise your computer monitor so the top of the screen is at eye level.
Take Breaks: Set a timer. Every 30 minutes, stand up and do a few Shoulder Rolls.
Stay Hydrated: Muscles need water to stay soft and flexible.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Q: Can physio cure neck and shoulder pain? A: Yes! Physiotherapy fixes the cause of the pain (like weak muscles or bad posture), not just the symptoms. It is a long-term solution.
Q: How long does it take to recover? A: It depends. A simple strain might heal in a few weeks. Chronic pain might take a few months of Sports Injury Rehabilitation.
Q: Is heat or ice better? A: Generally, use Ice for new, sharp injuries (first 48 hours) to reduce swelling. Use Heat for old, stiff, aching muscles to relax them.
Q: Can I do physio at home? A: You can do exercises at home, but you should see a physio first to learn the correct way to do them. We also offer Online Physiotherapy if you can’t visit us!

blocks.x: Do you feel a sharp pinch or a dull ache in your left shoulder? It can be scary when your shoulder hurts, especially on the left side.
But don’t worry! Most of the time, it is just your body telling you that something needs a little rest or care.
In this guide, we will look at what causes left shoulder pain, the symptoms to watch for, and how you can feel better fast.
What Are the Most Common Left Shoulder Pain Symptoms?
Before we look at the causes, let’s see how the pain feels. You might notice:
Stiffness: It feels hard to move your arm up or sideways.
Weakness: You struggle to lift a bag or even a glass of water.
Swelling: The area looks puffy or red.
Popping Sounds: You hear a “click” when you move.
Numbness: A “pins and needles” feeling going down your arm.
1. Common Injuries (The Most Likely Reasons)
Most left shoulder pain causes come from simple things we do every day, like playing sports or lifting something heavy.
Rotator Cuff Tears
Your shoulder has a group of muscles called the rotator cuff. If you lift something too heavy, these muscles can get a small tear. It makes your arm feel very weak.
Frozen Shoulder
This is when your shoulder joint gets “stuck.” It becomes very stiff and hurts a lot when you try to move it.
Shoulder Impingement
This happens when the bones in your shoulder pinch the soft muscles. It usually hurts most when you reach overhead.
Need Help? Our experts at Sports Injury Rehabilitation can help you move again without pain.
2. Left Shoulder and Arm Pain Causes: Is it a Bone Issue?
Sometimes the pain isn’t in the muscle, but in the bones or joints.
Arthritis: This is “wear and tear.” As we get older, the cushion between our bones wears away. This causes Arthritis Pain.
Bursitis: There are tiny liquid sacs in your shoulder that act like pillows. If they get swollen, it hurts to move.
Fractures: A small crack in the bone from a fall can cause sudden, sharp pain.
3. Surprising Facts: Can Anxiety Cause Pain in Left Arm and Shoulder?
Yes, it can! When you are very stressed or worried, your muscles tighten up.
Most people hold their stress in their neck and shoulders. This “tension” can make your left shoulder feel tight and painful. It’s your brain’s way of reacting to stress.
4. Can Overeating Cause Pain in Left Shoulder?
This might sound strange, but can overeating causes pain in left shoulder? The answer is yes.

When you eat too much, or if you have gas or gallbladder issues, the “phrenic nerve” can get irritated. This nerve goes from your stomach area up to your shoulder. Your brain gets confused and thinks the pain is coming from your left shoulder!
5. When Should I Worry? (Heart vs. Muscle)
Since it is the left side, many people worry about their heart.
Muscle Pain: Usually hurts more when you move or touch the spot.
Heart-Related Pain: Usually feels like a heavy weight on your chest, and the pain doesn’t change when you move your arm.
If you feel chest pressure, shortness of breath, or cold sweats, call an emergency doctor immediately.
How to Treat Left Shoulder Pain at Home
If your pain is mild, try the PRICE method:
Protect: Don’t lift anything heavy.
Rest: Give your arm a break.
Ice: Use a cold pack for 15 minutes to stop swelling.
Compress: Use a soft bandage if it feels unstable.
Elevate: Keep your shoulder propped up with pillows.
For long-term relief, Online Physiotherapy is a great way to get exercises from home.
FAQs: People Also Ask
Why does my left shoulder hurt at night? This is often due to bursitis or a rotator cuff injury. When you lie down, the pressure on the joint increases.
How long does shoulder pain last? A simple strain might get better in a week. However, a frozen shoulder can take months without Professional Treatment.
Can a neck problem cause left shoulder pain? Yes! A pinched nerve in your neck can send pain signals straight to your shoulder and arm.

blocks.x: Is your shoulder killing you after a chest day?
You walked into the gym feeling strong. You crushed your bench press, did your overhead presses, and felt a great “pump.” But now, a day later, you can barely lift your arm to wash your hair.
Is it just soreness? Or did you actually injure your shoulder joint?

At Threads Physio, we see this every single day. The shoulder is the most mobile joint in your body it’s like a golf ball sitting on a tiny tee. This makes it great for moving in circles, but terrible for stability. One wrong move, or one heavy lift with bad form, and you’re in pain.

In this guide, we will break down exactly why you have shoulder joint pain after gym, the difference between “good pain” and “bad pain,” and the best exercises to fix it so you can get back to training.
1. Good Pain vs. Bad Pain: How to Tell the Difference
Before you panic, let’s figure out what you’re feeling. Not all pain is an injury.
The “Good” Pain (DOMS)
This stands for Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.
When it starts: Usually 12 to 24 hours after your workout.
What it feels like: A dull ache, stiffness, or “tightness” in the muscles (deltoids).
The Test: If you gently massage the muscle and it feels better, it’s likely just DOMS. It means your muscles are growing!
The “Bad” Pain (Injury)
This is what we need to worry about.
When it starts: Can happen during the lift (a pop or snap) or wake you up at night with a throb.
What it feels like: Sharp, shooting, pinching, or stabbing pain deep inside the joint.
The Test: If the pain stops you from moving your arm, or if it hurts inside the socket (not just the muscle), it could be an injury.
Pro Tip: If your pain keeps you awake at night, that is a classic red flag for a rotator cuff issue. You should Book a Free Consultation with us immediately.
2. Why Does My Shoulder Hurt After the Gym? (5 Common Causes)
You didn’t just wake up in pain for no reason. Here are the top 5 reasons gym-goers destroy their shoulders.
1. The “Ego Lift” (Lifting Too Heavy)

We’ve all been there. You want to hit a PR (Personal Record), so you load up the bar. But your rotator cuff muscles are tiny compared to your chest or back. If the weight is too heavy, your big muscles take over, and the tiny stabilizers in your shoulder get crushed.
2. Bad Form (Technique)
Flaring Elbows: On bench press, if your elbows are flared out at 90 degrees, you are grinding your tendons.
Behind-the-Neck Press: This puts huge stress on the front of your shoulder capsule. Avoid it unless you have perfect mobility.
3. Muscle Imbalances

Do you train your chest 3 times a week but your back only once? This pulls your shoulders forward (slouching). When your shoulders are rounded, there is less space in the joint, leading to impingement (pinching).
4. Skipping the Warm-up
Walking on the treadmill is not a shoulder warm-up. You need to get blood flowing to the rotator cuff before you touch heavy weights.
5. Overtraining
Shoulders are involved in almost every upper body movement (Chest day, Back day, even some Leg days). If you don’t give them rest days, they will break down.
3. Common Shoulder Injuries from Lifting
If your pain isn’t going away after 3 days, it might be one of these common gym injuries.
Shoulder Impingement (The “Pinch”)
This is the most common gym injury. It happens when the tendons of your rotator cuff get pinched between your arm bone and your shoulder blade.
Symptoms: Pain when lifting your arm to the side or overhead.
Fix: You need to open up that space through posture correction and rehab.
Rotator Cuff Tears
Your rotator cuff is a group of 4 small muscles that hold your arm in the socket.
Symptoms: Deep ache in the shoulder, weakness, and trouble sleeping on that side.
Cause: Repetitive overhead lifting or a sudden heavy jerk.
Biceps Tendinitis
The biceps muscle isn’t just for looking good in t-shirts; it attaches inside your shoulder joint.
Symptoms: Pain in the front of the shoulder that travels down the arm.
Cause: Too many curls or heavy bench pressing.
Weightlifter’s Shoulder (AC Joint)
This affects the bony bump on top of your shoulder (where the collarbone meets the shoulder).
Symptoms: Pain right on top of the shoulder, especially when you cross your arm over your chest.
4. Immediate Relief: What to Do Right Now
If you are in pain right now, follow the R.I.C.E. method for the first 48 hours:
R – Rest: Stop lifting! Do not try to “push through” shoulder pain. You will make it worse.
I – Ice: Apply an ice pack for 15-20 minutes every few hours to reduce swelling.
C – Compression: Use a light shoulder wrap if it feels comfortable.
E – Elevation: Try to keep your shoulder propped up with pillows when sleeping.
Home Remedy: Some physios recommend sleeping on your “good” side with a pillow hugged against your chest to keep the injured shoulder in a neutral position.
5. The Best Exercises to Fix & Prevent Shoulder Pain
Note: If moving your arm causes sharp pain, stop and call us. These exercises are for rehab and prevention, not for acute tears.
1. Doorway Stretch (Opens the Chest)
Tight chest muscles pull your shoulders forward, causing pain.
Stand in a doorway.
Place your forearms on the doorframe at 90 degrees.
Lean forward gently until you feel a stretch in your chest.
Hold for 30 seconds.
2. Wall Slides
Great for posture and rotator cuff health.
Stand with your back against a wall.
Put your arms up like a “goal post” (elbows and wrists touching the wall).
Slide your hands up the wall as high as you can without your back leaving the wall.
Slide back down. Repeat 10 times.
3. Thread the Needle
A yoga move that is amazing for shoulder mobility.
Start on all fours (hands and knees).
Reach one arm underneath your body and across to the other side.
Lower your shoulder to the floor gently.
Hold for 30 seconds.
4. Crossover Arm Stretch
Pull one arm across your chest with the other hand.
Keep your shoulder down (don’t shrug).
Hold for 30 seconds.
5. Rotator Cuff External Rotation
Hold a light resistance band or a small water bottle.
Keep your elbow glued to your side at 90 degrees.
Rotate your hand outwards away from your belly.
Repeat 15 times on each side.
6. How Threads Physio Can Help You
At Threads Physio, we specialize in sports injuries. We don’t just treat the pain; we find the cause.
When you visit our clinic in Gurgaon (or consult us online), we check:
Your Posture: Are your shoulders rounded?
Your Biomechanics: How do you move? Check our Bio-Mechanical Assessment.
Your Strength: Is one side weaker than the other?

Q: Should I work out with shoulder pain? A: If it is just soreness (DOMS), yes, you can do light cardio or legs. If it is sharp joint pain, NO. Rest the upper body until the pain is gone.
Q: How long does a shoulder strain take to heal? A: Minor strains can heal in 2 weeks. A rotator cuff tear or severe impingement can take 3 to 6 months without proper rehab.
Q: Is heat or ice better for shoulder pain? A: Use Ice for the first 48 hours to stop inflammation. Use Heat after that to loosen up tight muscles and stiff joints.

blocks.x: Do you love doing pushups but hate the sharp pain in your shoulder afterwards? You are not alone.
Pushups are one of the best exercises for building strength. But if you feel shoulder pain after pushups, it can be really scary. You might wonder, “Did I tear a muscle?” or “Is my form wrong?”
Don’t worry. In this guide, we will explain exactly why your shoulder hurts, how to fix your pushup form, and how to get relief fast. We have written this for you, so it is super easy to understand.
Why Do Pushups Hurt My Shoulders? (The Simple Truth)
To understand the pain, we first need to look at how your shoulder works.

Imagine your shoulder joint is like a golf ball sitting on a tee. It can move in almost any direction! This is great for throwing a ball or reaching a high shelf, but it also makes the shoulder very unstable.

When you do a pushup, you put a lot of weight on this unstable joint. If your muscles (called the rotator cuff) are not strong enough to hold the “ball” on the “tee,” your shoulder bones might rub against each other. This rubbing causes that pinch or ache you feel.
5 Common Reasons for Shoulder Pain After Pushups
If your front shoulder pain after pushups is bothering you, it is usually because of one of these 5 reasons.
1. Your Elbows Are “Chicken Winging”
This is the #1 mistake! If your elbows flare out wide (like 90 degrees) when you go down, you are grinding your shoulder bones together. This puts huge stress on your joints.
2. Your Hands Are in the Wrong Spot
Are your hands too far forward? Or maybe too wide?
Too Wide: Stretches the front of your shoulder too much.
Too Forward: Puts extra pressure on your rotator cuff.
3. Weak Shoulder Muscles
Your big chest muscles might be strong, but the small stabilizing muscles inside your shoulder might be weak. If they are weak, they can’t protect your joint during a heavy pushup.
4. You Are Doing Too Much, Too Soon
Did you try to do 50 pushups when you usually only do 10? This is called “Overuse.” Your muscles need time to rest and repair. If you don’t rest, you get inflammation (swelling).
5. Lack of Mobility

Can you scratch your back easily? If your shoulders are stiff or tight, forcing them into a pushup position will cause pain. This is often why you might feel pain between shoulder and chest after pushup.
Pro Tip: Need a professional check-up? Book a Bio-Mechanical Assessment with our experts at Threads Physio.
Is It Just Soreness or an Injury?
How do you know if you are just sore from a good workout or if you are actually hurt? Use this simple table to check.
If you have sharp pain, do not push through it!
How to Fix Your Pushup Form (The 45-Degree Rule)
You can reduce shoulder pain after pushups instantly by fixing your form. Here is the golden rule:
The Arrow Shape (Not the T-Shape)
Look at yourself in a mirror from above (or record a video).
WRONG (T-Shape): Your body looks like a letter ‘T’. Your elbows are straight out.
RIGHT (Arrow Shape): Your elbows should be tucked in at a 45-degree angle. Your body should look like an Arrow (↑).
Correct Hand Placement
Place your hands directly under your shoulders.
Spread your fingers wide to grip the floor.
Screw your hands into the ground (imagine trying to open two jars with your hands on the floor). This turns on your back muscles and protects your shoulders.
Immediate Relief: How to Treat Shoulder Pain at Home
If your shoulder is throbbing right now, follow these steps:
Rest: Stop doing pushups for a few days. Let the inflammation go down.
Ice: Put an ice pack on your shoulder for 15-20 minutes to cool down the pain.
Gentle Movement: Don’t keep your arm totally still. Gently swing it to keep blood flowing.
Check Your Pillow: Sometimes, sleeping on a sore shoulder makes it worse. Try sleeping on your back.
For chronic stiffness, you might need specific treatments like Acupuncture Treatment or Shoulder Pain Treatment.
Best Pushup Alternatives (While You Heal)
You don’t have to stop exercising completely! Try these safer versions while your shoulder heals.
1. Neutral Grip Pushups
Use dumbbells or pushup handles. Hold them so your palms face each other. This keeps your elbows tucked in naturally and takes pressure off the shoulder joint.
2. Wall Pushups
Stand away from a wall and do pushups against it. This is much easier and puts very little weight on your shoulders. It is great for practicing your form.
3. Knee Pushups
Drop to your knees. This reduces the weight you are lifting by about 50%. Focus on keeping your back straight and your core tight.
Prevention: Bulletproof Your Shoulders
To never feel top shoulder bone is paining after doing pike pushups again, you need to prepare your body.
